title: Texas Professional Ethics Committee Opinion 705: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
author: Professional Ethics Committee for the State Bar of Texas

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The opinion accepts that generative AI can improve legal-service efficiency and that verification remains necessary, then materially develops the cluster’s pricing analysis by specifying the hourly-billing consequence: lawyers may charge for time actually spent using and checking AI output, but not for hours saved through automation; under hourly arrangements, those efficiency gains benefit the client.
qs: In most typical hourly arrangements (depending on the agreement), a lawyer will likely be able to charge the client for the actual time the lawyer spends using a generative AI program for purposes of the representation, including to refine the program’s outputs and check the work.
A lawyer may not, however, charge hourly fees for the time that was “saved” by using the generative AI program.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion accepts selective, human-led deployment and materially develops the cluster’s verification and governance claims through Texas-specific duties of technological competence, confidentiality, lawyer accountability, court-rule compliance and honest billing. It treats AI output as assistance requiring use-specific risk assessment and substantive human review, rather than autonomous legal competence.
qs: The extent to which Rule 1.05 is implicated by the use of generative AI will depend on how a given program works and how a lawyer uses it.

The best practice here, as with many other efficiency-enhancing tools in the law: AI-generated outputs can be used as a starting point for a lawyer’s work, but must always be carefully analyzed for accuracy and quality.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: Texas Opinion 705 directly supports conditional AI assistance subject to substantive human verification and retained lawyer responsibility. It also reinforces the cluster’s account that existing professional duties govern AI use while court-specific disclosure or prohibition rules materially differ.
qs: So, the Committee will say it again: lawyers are responsible for the work product they submit regardless of who (or what) does the original research and drafting.

Some courts have issued standing orders or local rules prohibiting the use of generative AI to draft legal filings or at least requiring certain forms of disclosure; others have declined to issue any such rules at all.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: Texas Opinion 705 strongly supports the cluster’s central proposition that lawyers remain accountable for AI-assisted work and must independently verify more than fabricated citations. It also aligns with the cluster’s technology-neutral application of existing duties, confidentiality safeguards, and recognition that courts differ on AI-specific disclosure or restrictions.
qs: So, the Committee will say it again: lawyers are responsible for the work product they submit regardless of who (or what) does the original research and drafting.

That said, a lawyer’s duties require more than merely detecting and eliminating false AI-generated results—the lawyer is ultimately responsible for ensuring that the content is accurate and supports the client’s interests.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The opinion supports the cluster’s emphasis on protection and accountability by recognizing useful legal applications while warning that convincing hallucinations can cause concrete harm and reaffirming lawyers’ continuing competence obligations. Its provisional, non-exhaustive framing also accords with the cluster’s refusal to treat current evidence or safeguards as settled.
qs: Indeed, many generative AI models have a tendency to “hallucinate,” or create inaccurate or made-up answers that sound convincing.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s copilot framing: AI output may be a starting point, but lawyers retain responsibility for verification, substantive judgment and final work product. It also reinforces the risks of hallucinations and the need to follow differing court-specific requirements, though it does not assess whether verification costs erase efficiency gains.

So, the Committee will say it again: lawyers are responsible for the work product they submit regardless of who (or what) does the original research and drafting.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The opinion squarely supports the cluster’s core framing: generative AI is an efficiency-enhancing aid whose outputs require careful human verification, while lawyers retain responsibility for accuracy, quality and client interests. It also supports tool-specific confidentiality controls and honest billing, though it does not empirically determine how much verification erodes efficiency gains.

The best practice here, as with many other efficiency-enhancing tools in the law: AI-generated outputs can be used as a starting point for a lawyer’s work, but must always be carefully analyzed for accuracy and quality.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: Texas Opinion 705 directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI does not displace lawyers’ professional responsibility and that verification must assess substantive accuracy, quality and client interests—not merely remove fabricated material. It also applies existing competence, candour, fairness and confidentiality duties, while offering little direct support for the cluster’s broader extension of accountability to institutional leaders.

kp.k: Opinion applies existing ethics principles to rapidly changing technology
kp.d: Responding to the State Bar of Texas’s Taskforce on Responsible AI in the Law, the Committee offers a high-level interpretation of Texas disciplinary obligations rather than an exhaustive treatment or empirical assessment. Its February 2025 guidance is expressly provisional as to technological risks, while restating ethical principles intended to remain useful as technology changes.
qs: So this opinion does not purport to address every ethical issue that might arise now or in the future.

This opinion is intended only to provide a snapshot of potential ethical concerns at the moment and a restatement of certain ethical principles for lawyers to use as a guide regardless of where the technology goes.

kp.k: AI assists legal tasks but introduces fabricated-output risks
kp.d: The Committee identifies contract review and management, due diligence, document review, research, and initial drafting as applications of legal-specific generative AI. It cites Mata v. Avianca, June 22, 2023, as a sanctions example illustrating fabricated judicial citations, not as evidence of a measured error rate or quantified productivity benefit.
qs: And some companies have designed generative AI tools specifically for the practice of law, to assist in tasks like contract review and management, due diligence, document review, research, and even initial drafting of letters, contracts, and briefs.
The most famous example at this point is a case where lawyers were sanctioned for submitting a brief that cited non-existent judicial opinions made up by ChatGPT.

kp.k: AI use requires competence, but adoption is not mandated
kp.d: The Committee interprets Texas Rule 1.01 as requiring lawyers who choose generative AI to maintain a reasonable, current understanding of its operation and risks, including inaccurate outputs, incomplete data, and confidentiality exposure. It considers mandatory adoption almost certainly unwarranted at present because the technology and cost-benefit assessment remain unsettled, while cautioning against unnecessarily avoiding technology that could save clients time and money.
qs: Rule 1.01 almost certainly does not *require* the use of generative AI for any particular purpose in the practice of law, especially at the present moment where the technology is still developing and the cost-benefit analysis remains somewhat unclear.
the lawyer must have a reasonable and current understanding of the technology

kp.k: Confidentiality risks depend on tools and prompting practices
kp.d: Texas Rule 1.05 protects both privileged information and other client-related information acquired during representation. General research may avoid disclosure, but prompts describing facts, legal theories, or arguments can expose confidential information, including privileged mental impressions. The Committee particularly warns that programs retaining inputs for self-learning may reveal them in later third-party responses; it presents this as a risk dependent on how the program operates.
qs: The extent to which Rule 1.05 is implicated by the use of generative AI will depend on how a given program works and how a lawyer uses it.
These exchanges could, if nothing else, expose the lawyer’s privileged mental impressions to the generative AI tool.

The use of such self-learning programs poses a risk that the confidential information a lawyer inputs to the program may be stored within the program and revealed in responses to future inquiries by third parties.

kp.k: Confidentiality protection requires vendor diligence and staff training
kp.d: Before using generative AI for client work, lawyers must understand the technology reasonably and take reasonable precautions to protect information. Drawing on its cloud-computing Opinion 680, the Committee recommends understanding operation, reviewing and potentially renegotiating terms, examining security against hacking as well as intentional disclosure, and training lawyers and staff. It calls for continuing vigilance rather than technological expertise.
qs: Before any lawyer uses a generative AI product for client work, the lawyer must understand to a reasonable degree how the technology works and must take reasonable precautions to ensure that any client confidential information is protected.
reviewing and potentially renegotiating the “terms of service” to which the lawyer submits when using the generative AI tool;
training lawyers and staff about how to appropriately use generative AI tools while protecting client confidential information.

kp.k: Disclosure and consent obligations remain context dependent
kp.d: The Committee explains that Texas Rules 1.05(c) and 1.05(d) may permit disclosure to service providers reasonably necessary for effective representation, provided lawyers are reasonably confident information will remain protected. If not satisfied about protection, lawyers should at minimum avoid confidential inputs without client consultation and consent. It reports California, ABA, and Florida guidance separately, while advising Texas lawyers to undertake thoughtful, circumstances-specific analysis rather than announcing universal consent for all AI use.
qs: But the lawyer can only do so if he or she is reasonably confident that the confidential character of the information will be respected and protected by the service provider.
If the lawyer is not so satisfied, the lawyer should—at a minimum—not input any confidential information to the program without client consultation and consent.

If a lawyer intends to use confidential information in conjunction with generative AI tools, the lawyer should consider informing clients about the associated risks and may need to secure client consent.

kp.k: Lawyers retain responsibility and must verify AI outputs
kp.d: The opinion treats generative AI as a starting point for lawyer work, not a substitute for professional responsibility. It analogizes reliance on AI to reliance on inexperienced or overconfident nonlawyer assistants under Texas Rule 5.03. Failure to verify can implicate competence, meritorious claims, candor, and fairness rules; review must address quality and client interests as well as fabricated content.
qs: lawyers are responsible for the work product they submit regardless of who (or what) does the original research and drafting.
AI-generated outputs can be used as a starting point for a lawyer’s work, but must always be carefully analyzed for accuracy and quality.

a lawyer’s duties require more than merely detecting and eliminating false AI-generated results—the lawyer is ultimately responsible for ensuring that the content is accurate and supports the client’s interests.

kp.k: Court-specific AI restrictions require separate attention
kp.d: Lawyers must track differing court requirements governing AI-assisted filings. The Committee contrasts the Northern District of Texas’s disclosure rule for AI-prepared briefs with the Fifth Circuit’s June 10, 2024 decision not to adopt a special rule, rather than presenting a uniform judicial approach.
qs: A lawyer must also be aware of how various courts treat the use of generative AI.

Some courts have issued standing orders or local rules prohibiting the use of generative AI to draft legal filings or at least requiring certain forms of disclosure; others have declined to issue any such rules at all.

kp.k: Hourly clients receive savings; verification time remains billable
kp.d: The Committee presents greater efficiency as a promising possibility, not a quantified finding. Under typical hourly agreements, subject to their terms, lawyers may likely bill actual time using AI, refining outputs, and checking work, but cannot charge for hours avoided. It supports this position with quoted D.C. and Florida ethics guidance, making the allocation of efficiency gains specifically dependent on hourly billing.
qs: In most typical hourly arrangements (depending on the agreement), a lawyer will likely be able to charge the client for the actual time the lawyer spends using a generative AI program for purposes of the representation, including to refine the program’s outputs and check the work.
A lawyer may not, however, charge hourly fees for the time that was “saved” by using the generative AI program.

kp.k: Per-use AI expenses may be reimbursed without general markup
kp.d: The Committee allows that clients may agree to reimburse per-use AI charges where legally permitted, analogizing them to traditional online research expenses. It qualifies this permission by generally limiting recovery to expenses actually incurred and paid to the provider.
qs: If the lawyer pays per use for a particular generative AI program, the lawyer may be able to collect those expenses from the client, as allowed by law and if the client accepts that arrangement.
The lawyer will generally not be permitted to recover more than the amount of expenses actually incurred and paid to the generative AI provider.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Texas Professional Ethics Committee presents generative AI as a potentially efficiency-enhancing aid to legal work, subject to continuing lawyer responsibility, confidentiality safeguards, and billing constraints.
pts.d: The Committee identifies applications in contract review and management, due diligence, document review, research, and initial drafting. It describes efficiency and client savings as possibilities rather than measured results. It says using AI requires technological understanding but almost certainly is not currently required by the duty of competence. AI-generated work must remain a starting point subject to human verification, not something lawyers can rely on blindly; responsibility extends beyond removing fabricated material to ensuring accuracy and supporting client interests. The Committee warns that prompts can expose confidential facts and privileged mental impressions, and that programs which retain and incorporate inputs may disclose them to third parties. Appropriate protections depend on the product and its use, with consultation or consent potentially necessary. For hourly work, lawyers may generally bill actual time spent using AI, refining outputs, and checking work, but not time saved. Per-use expenses may be recoverable when legally permitted and accepted by the client, generally without charging more than the actual expense.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The opinion rests primarily on ethical rules, prior opinions, and a sanctions case, not quantitative evidence of AI performance or economic effects.
pts.d: The Committee cites Mata v. Avianca as a concrete instance of sanctions for submitting fabricated judicial citations. This is a hallucination-related court incident, not a measured model error rate. Its technological-competence and confidentiality analysis draws on Texas Rules 1.01 and 1.05 and earlier Texas opinions concerning cloud computing, metadata, and third-party services. Its verification analysis invokes Texas Rules 1.01, 3.01, 3.03, and 3.04 and analogizes to responsibilities regarding nonlawyer assistants under Texas Rule 5.03. It cites Northern District of Texas and Fifth Circuit approaches to illustrate differing court requirements. Its billing analysis draws on other ethics opinions, including D.C., Florida, ABA, and Texas guidance. The California, ABA, and Florida positions on disclosure or consent are comparative authorities, not a categorical Texas consent requirement. The opinion provides no benchmark, productivity measurement, quantified cost saving, or labour-market forecast.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The February 2025 opinion expressly offers a provisional snapshot, with obligations conditional on the tool, its use, and the applicable representation and billing arrangements.
pts.d: The Committee describes rapidly changing technology and warns that technological or industry changes may resolve some concerns. It provides no dated prediction of future adoption or displacement. The near-term position that AI use is almost certainly not required is qualified by developing technology and an unclear cost-benefit analysis. Competence and verification obligations apply when lawyers choose to use AI. Confidentiality implications depend on what the program does and what information the lawyer supplies; general research may avoid disclosure entirely. Where protection is uncertain, the Committee says confidential information should not be entered without at least client consultation and consent. Disclosure through service providers can be permissible under the applicable Texas rules when the lawyer is reasonably confident that confidentiality will be protected. Billing actual AI-related time depends on the hourly agreement; reimbursement of per-use costs depends on legal permissibility and client acceptance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are Texas lawyers, their staff and clients, with courts also affected by AI-assisted filings.
pts.d: Texas lawyers remain accountable for AI-assisted work and must understand relevant technology, protect information, verify outputs, comply with court-specific requirements, and bill accurately. Lawyers and staff need training on confidentiality-preserving use. Clients may receive more efficient services and lower hourly charges when actual work time falls, but face information-exposure and inaccurate-work risks and may need to participate in decisions about consent and expenses. Courts face fabricated citations and other unreliable submissions. The opinion does not distinguish effects by firm size or legal-market segment, or predict changes in staffing, hiring, professional displacement, or access to justice.
